cards.title: Tight quantum query lower bounds for uniformity testing
cards.formal: Does testing whether an unknown distribution p on [d] is exactly uniform or has total variation distance greater than ε from uniform require Ω(min{d^{1/3}/ε^{4/3}, √d/ε}) quantum queries to a synthesizer for p, with success probability at least 0.99 on every promised input? The bound is uniform in d≥2 and 0<ε≤1/4; this explicit small-error range avoids the empty or near-maximal-distance promises implicit in an unrestricted reading of the source.
cards.why: Would identify the optimal joint dependence on domain size and accuracy for one of the basic distribution-testing tasks with coherent sampler access, clarifying the extent of quantum advantage over classical samples.
cards.status_note: Conjecture, access definitions, version record and later-result searches checked through 12 September 2026. No matching general quantum-query lower bound was located; classical uniformity and quantum-state measurement results use different access models.

progress.text: The TQC paper supplies the matching candidate upper bound and states its optimality as Conjecture 2.

sentences: A quantum tester must distinguish exact uniformity from a distribution whose total variation distance exceeds ε.
It can invoke a coherent sampler, its inverse and a controlled invocation.
The best known query upper bound is the smaller of d^{1/3}/ε^{4/3} and √d/ε.
The question is whether every tester must pay this cost in the worst case across both parameters.
The source also proposes a stronger lower bound for string oracles, whose extra structure is kept separate from the main target.

references.title: Uniformity Testing When You Have the Source Code
references.authors: Canonne, Clément L.; Kothari, Robin; O'Donnell, Ryan

cards.definitions: Write [d]={1,…,d}, u_d(i)=1/d and d_TV(p,u_d)=(1/2)Σ_i|p_i−1/d|. The algorithm receives d and ε and oracle access to a unitary U_p satisfying U_p|0^k⟩=Σ_i√p_i|i⟩|ψ_i⟩, where each garbage state |ψ_i⟩ is normalized. The extension of U_p away from |0^k⟩ and its garbage states are arbitrary; the tester must work for every valid oracle satisfying the promise. A query is one application of U_p, U_p† or controlled-U_p; intervening quantum operations, ancillas and measurements are unrestricted and do not count toward query complexity. The code is used as a black box: the tester does not get a classical description to inspect for free. Let Q(d,ε) be the minimum worst-case number of such queries among testers whose probability of the correct yes/no output is at least 0.99 for every oracle with p=u_d or d_TV(p,u_d)>ε, taking the worst case over allowed oracle-register sizes. No guarantee is required in the intermediate gap. The conjecture asks for an absolute c>0 with Q(d,ε)≥c min{d^{1/3}ε^{-4/3},d^{1/2}ε^{-1}} throughout the stated parameter range, up to conventional finite asymptotic exceptions.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the uniform two-parameter lower bound in this oracle model, or refute it by a tester with a smaller worst-case asymptotic query complexity in a valid parameter regime. Lower bounds for classical samples, one particular algorithm, constant ε only, or a restricted family of quantum testers do not establish the full claim.

context_blocks.title: Running a sampler backwards is extra information
context_blocks.text: Ordinary sample access reveals only independent outcomes. Coherent access to a sampler and its inverse permits interference between executions. This can reduce the number of calls needed to detect a departure from uniformity; a classical sample lower bound therefore does not automatically apply.

context_blocks.title: The upper bound has two regimes
context_blocks.text: The paper establishes O(min{d^{1/3}/ε^{4/3},√d/ε}) queries. The terms cross at ε=d^{-1/2}: the first governs larger errors and the second smaller errors. The question asks whether any quantum tester can improve this full dependence.

context_blocks.title: Separate lower bounds leave a gap
context_blocks.text: The source recalls Ω(d^{1/3}) queries for constant ε and Ω(1/ε) already on a two-element domain. Knowing both separately does not yield their conjectured joint dependence. For example, at ε=d^{-1/2} the target is Ω(d).

context_blocks.title: A stronger variant fixes a special oracle structure
context_blocks.text: For a string x∈[d]^m, the standard oracle maps |j,z⟩ to |j,z⊕x_j⟩ and defines p_i=|{j:x_j=i}|/m. The authors also conjecture the same lower bound even with this structure available, in the worst case over m and x. This is a stronger claim than the arbitrary-synthesizer target selected here; fixed small m can cap the cost through reading the entire string.

cards.title: Do symmetric IPS lower bounds imply a symmetric VP–VNP separation?
cards.formal: For suitably defined symmetric analogues of VP and VNP, would superpolynomial lower bounds on symmetric Ideal Proof System refutations of unsatisfiable Boolean CNF formulas imply that symmetric VP differs from symmetric VNP? The source poses the development of those analogue classes as part of the question; they have not been specified here.
cards.why: Would connect structural restrictions on algebraic proofs with a corresponding arithmetic complexity separation, giving a precise algebraic interpretation of the power lost by requiring proofs to respect symmetries.
cards.status_note: Source definitions, final question, version record and subsequent searches checked through 12 September 2026. The necessary symmetric algebraic classes remain unspecified in the source; no complete matching formulation and resolution was located.

progress.text: The MFCS paper defines symmetric IPS and poses the VP/VNP analogue question after its proof-size, degree and linearity results.

importance.reason: A structural connection between algebraic proof complexity and symmetric arithmetic circuit classes; existing numerical score retained.

sentences: An IPS refutation encodes unsatisfiability as a polynomial identity computed by an arithmetic circuit.
A symmetric refutation must let every permitted instance relabeling extend to the circuit gates.
The source asks whether proving such refutations require superpolynomial size would separate symmetric analogues of VP and VNP.
The ordinary IPS-to-algebraic-complexity connection motivates this proposed implication.
The appropriate symmetric algebraic classes and their compatibility with the formula families still need to be defined.

cards.definitions: A Boolean CNF is a conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of literals. Over a fixed field K, encode each clause by the product of the factors that equal one when its literals are false, set that product to zero, and add x_i²−x_i=0 for Boolean variables. For example, x∨¬y becomes (1−x)y=0. Let f_1(x),…,f_m(x) be the resulting polynomials. An IPS certificate is a polynomial C(x,y) with C(x,0)=0 and C(x,f_1(x),…,f_m(x))=1 as polynomial identities; an IPS refutation is an arithmetic circuit over K computing C. A group Γ acts by permutations of the x variables and preserves the polynomial axiom set; it then permutes y_i according to the induced permutation of f_i. The circuit is Γ-symmetric when each group permutation extends to a permutation of its gates preserving wires, operation labels and field constants. Polynomial invariance of its output alone is weaker than this circuit requirement. Size is measured by circuit gates with the instance-size floor; a superpolynomial family lower bound excludes any one polynomial bound in encoded formula size. In the ordinary nonsymmetric setting, VP consists of polynomial-degree polynomial families in polynomially many variables having polynomial-size arithmetic circuits. VNP consists of families expressible as a sum over polynomially many Boolean witness variables of such a VP family. How to impose compatible symmetries on these families and on the summation is a missing part of the proposed analogue.
cards.answer_criterion: Specify and justify the symmetric algebraic classes and compatible CNF/group families, then prove or refute the stated implication under those fixed definitions. A lower bound for invariant polynomials, for a bounded-degree IPS fragment, or only for Hilbert-like certificates does not automatically establish a lower bound for the full symmetric IPS system.

context_blocks.title: A short algebraic identity certifies impossibility
context_blocks.text: If all axioms f_i vanished at a common Boolean assignment, substituting them into a valid certificate would give both C(x,0)=0 and C(x,f(x))=1. The certificate rules out that assignment by a polynomial identity, with its arithmetic circuit providing a compact representation.

context_blocks.title: Symmetry is a restriction on the proof itself
context_blocks.text: Relabeling an instance must extend through the entire circuit. Two circuits computing the same invariant polynomial can differ in whether such gate permutations exist. This makes symmetric proof complexity a distinct question from ordinary circuit complexity.

context_blocks.title: The ordinary implication motivates the question
context_blocks.text: The source recalls the Grochow–Pitassi connection: superpolynomial unrestricted IPS lower bounds for Boolean CNFs imply VP≠VNP. Restricting proofs to symmetric circuits does not by itself establish the analogous conclusion for newly defined symmetric classes.

context_blocks.title: Known fragment separations do not settle the full target
context_blocks.text: The paper compares symmetric proof size, degree and linearity, and obtains nontrivial upper bounds for several standard formula families. A separation between those proof fragments is not yet a separation of the symmetric algebraic classes asked for in the final question.

notes: Recovered the defined symmetric proof system and separated it from the undeveloped algebraic classes.
statement_review.remaining_issue: The source does not define the proposed symmetric analogues of VP and VNP. A complete target must fix the base field, variable and group-action families, size/degree conventions, and how Boolean summation and any relevant reductions respect those actions. The source also leaves the corresponding CNF-family and symmetry quantifiers implicit. Merely assigning names to classes chosen to make the implication true would not recover its intended content.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
